video_title: Bitcoin Wins By Simply Not Playing The Time Game
gist: Jordi Visser argues the S&P 500 is undergoing multiple compression because earnings are compounding ~30%+ year-over-year while the index annualizes near 20%, that inflation is contextually far weaker than tariffs/oil/money-printing would imply because AI-driven margin gains are turning deflationary, and that the real investable frontier is the merger of AI agents with tokenized finance (Figure, Robinhood, Coinbase, PayPal) which collapses settlement time and destroys middlemen. Despite the Bitcoin-centric title, Bitcoin is discussed only briefly as a closing philosophical point — that it is the only asset that 'does not suffer from time' — while the bulk of the hour is AI equities, inflation mechanics, LLM-lab valuation math, and incumbent-vs-AI-native disruption.

themes.theme: AI Equity Drawdown and Recovery Mechanics

insights.claim: S&P 500 earnings are tracking above 30% year-over-year growth while the index itself is annualizing around 20%, meaning the 2026 rally is happening through multiple compression rather than multiple expansion.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Equity upside is being funded by earnings, not sentiment — a rare setup where a rising market is getting cheaper, which argues against the 'bubble' framing and for staying long as long as earnings hold.
insights.quote: we're headed for year-over-year at above 30%. The S&P, when you annualize the performance, we're going to come in, assuming that we continue at this pace, somewhere in around 20%

insights.claim: Two-year Treasury yields remain well above the Fed funds rate and the market has begun pricing in rate hikes, which Visser considers anomalous given a negative payroll print, soft PPI, soft retail sales, and downside inflation surprises.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: If hike pricing unwinds toward the actual data, the front end of the curve is mispriced and duration plus rate-sensitive equities get a tailwind.
insights.quote: I think it's actually kind of amazing that we have rate hikes built in at all. Two-year rates are still well above the Fed funds rate right now.

insights.claim: The economy overall is fine but almost all of the growth is concentrated inside AI, which is why broad macro prints look soft while equity earnings accelerate.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Macro-driven allocation frameworks will keep producing bearish signals that miss the market — exposure must be to the AI complex specifically, not to the index-as-economy proxy.
insights.quote: The economy is good, but most of the good is happening within inside AI

insights.claim: The Kospi 200 broke down hard on the chart but is still up roughly 70% year-to-date, illustrating that AI-complex drawdowns now compress into one month what used to take nine.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Chart-based risk management calibrated to older cycle speeds will shake investors out of positions that are still massively profitable; size positions for compressed volatility, not for the drawdown's optics.
insights.quote: it broke down hard. It kind of looks a lot like Bitcoin. It just happened in a month as opposed to 9 months. But here's the reality, it's still up 70% year-to-date.

insights.claim: The 'situational awareness' episode functioned as a market-clearing capitulation event in AI, with some hedge funds down 25–30% in a single month, which is what improved forward risk-reward rather than any identifiable price bottom.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Watch for forced-deleveraging magnitude, not price levels, as the signal that a growth-equity drawdown has exhausted itself.
insights.quote: We've seen some hedge funds be down 25-30% for the month.

insights.claim: The AI rally is advancing on low volume while the selloff came on high volume, a signature Visser reads as demand having absorbed supply at lower prices and late buyers now being locked out.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Low-volume advances are conventionally read as weak; Visser inverts that after a capitulation — a rule that flags the current tape as strong rather than suspect.
insights.quote: we've seen it go up and the volume has been very, very low. The The volume getting out was much higher, which I highlighted on the videos. Those are capitulation type events.

insights.claim: Visser's 10-name most-correlated AI basket — including Nvidia, Intel for CPUs, Marvell for optical, Caterpillar and Corning — has retraced more than 50% of the drawdown, and the absence of any pullback is preventing sidelined investors from re-entering.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: The AI trade is broader than semis — industrial and materials names like Caterpillar and Corning are core AI infrastructure exposure and screen cheaper than pure-play chips.
insights.quote: That one has bounced back more than 50% of the fall. And part of the strength that has been there is it's not allowing anyone to get back in because there's really not been any correction.

insights.claim: Visser rebought Micron above his own exit price because new information changed the odds: better-than-expected earnings, newly signed long-term agreements that de-cyclicalize the earnings stream, and rising DRAM prices amid accelerating compute demand.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Long-term supply agreements are the specific catalyst to underwrite memory names at a structurally higher multiple — the historical cyclical discount on Micron may no longer apply.
insights.quote: they signed long-term agree- agreements, meaning they're not going to have cyclical earnings the way they did in the past

insights.claim: Fears that open-source models would reduce compute demand were wrong — compute demand has actually accelerated and DRAM pricing has risen.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: The open-source-kills-capex bear case is a fadeable narrative; memory and compute suppliers are the direct beneficiaries of it being wrong.
insights.quote: the compute situation everyone started to worry because of the open source where to me the compute demand is actually accelerated and DRAM prices have gone higher

insights.claim: Investors should judge analysts on whether they update to new information rather than on whether a prediction proved right, since a Bayesian mindset is the only durable edge in fast-moving markets.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Screen research providers on revision behavior, not hit rate — stubbornness in a compressed-information regime is the real risk factor.
insights.quote: I don't critique people for making predictions. I critique them for being stubborn and for not adjusting to new information and changing as the data changes.

insights.claim: Visser expects investors to stay bearish through the entire AI advance because they do not understand the technology, making persistent skepticism a structural feature rather than a top signal.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Sentiment surveys will not mark the top of this cycle; use earnings deceleration rather than positioning or sentiment as the exit trigger.
insights.quote: So we'll be climbing a wall of AI worry for a long time.

themes.theme: Contextual Inflation and the AI Deflation Impulse

insights.claim: Core CPI has gone from 2.6% year-over-year at the end of last year to roughly 2.5% now, essentially the cycle low, despite tariffs, soaring oil, higher fertilizer costs, and accelerating nominal GDP that should all have pushed it far higher.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: The correct read is not the absolute level versus the 2% target but the enormous negative residual versus what the inputs imply — that residual is the tradeable signal.
insights.quote: Inflation to me is something that should be higher than it is today based on everything we're seeing.

insights.claim: AI-driven margin improvement is beginning to show up as consumer price deflation, with insurance the leading edge as AI-native startups like Lemonade undercut incumbents on car insurance pricing.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Watch insurance, and then any high-overhead service sector, for the first visible AI deflation prints — incumbents in those verticals face margin compression before AI shows up in their own P&L.
insights.quote: if every company was using AI in their business and their margins were improving, then they'd be able to lower prices

insights.claim: Oil is likely to end the year near $65 despite an ongoing war, because the market has begun de-rating Strait of Hormuz risk as new pipelines get built — an event priced into three-year forwards even though it has not happened yet.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Geopolitical oil risk premium is structurally shrinking; the war-driven long-oil trade has a shorter shelf life than the headlines suggest, and that removes a key inflation input.
insights.quote: if the oil market thinks it's going to be here in 3 years, which they do, well, then all of a sudden this Hormuz thing doesn't matter for 3-year prices, it just matters for 1-year price

insights.claim: On a three-year horizon Visser believes inflation faces substantial headwinds to moving higher, and he deliberately refuses to trade the current monthly print.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A structurally disinflationary three-year view supports duration, long-duration growth equities, and against consensus positioning for a second inflation wave.
insights.quote: I get caught more on where do I think everything will be in 3 years from now, and I think inflation is going to have a lot of headwinds to go higher.

insights.claim: The persistence of consumer price anger traces back to the 2020 money printing rather than current policy, illustrated by a five-year-old Tesla whose annual insurance premium now runs 5–10% of the car's current value.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Level-based price pain, not rate-of-change inflation, is what drives the political economy — meaning disinflation prints will not fix consumer sentiment or the electoral pressure on the Fed.

insights.claim: Kevin Warsh is framing policy for Congress around a forward-looking view rather than the current above-target reading, which Visser reads as the contextual approach to inflation gaining institutional ground.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A forward-looking Fed leadership posture is dovish relative to a backward-looking reaction function — relevant to the hikes currently priced into the front end.

themes.theme: Time as the Core Investment Variable

insights.claim: Bitcoin's core advantage is not innovation but that it is the only major asset not denominated in time, which is why Visser calls it the S&P 500 of ten years from now.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Reframes the Bitcoin case away from adoption-curve arguments toward a structural one — every cash-flow asset gets re-rated as growth rates compress, while a non-time-based asset does not.
insights.quote: The reason Bitcoin, to me, is the ultimate choice, it is the S&P 500 of 10 years from now, is not because of anything special about it from an innovation perspective? It's because it doesn't suffer from time because it's not based on time.

insights.claim: Year-over-year measurement is an artifact of human time that breaks down when a company can complete in one quarter the transaction volume it used to take a year to do.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Comparing an AI-native or tokenized business to an incumbent on a YoY basis systematically understates the gap; investors need shorter measurement windows to see the divergence early.
insights.quote: Because we measure things in human time, year-over-year. Why do we care about a year?

insights.claim: Business cycles that used to run ten years are now completing in three months, which means information decays before an investor can finish processing it.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Research cadence itself becomes an edge — slow institutional processes are structurally disadvantaged in a regime where facts expire this fast.
insights.quote: We're now doing what used to take 10 years in 3 months.

insights.claim: AI operates at a speed that neither human brains nor corporate organizations can absorb, and stablecoin volumes and transaction counts are already running at unprecedented paces that will keep intensifying.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Stablecoin transaction volume is the leading indicator to track for the AI-agent-meets-payments convergence trade.
insights.quote: The stablecoin volumes and the transactions are going already at paces that we've never seen before.

themes.theme: Tokenized Finance and the Velocity Trade

insights.claim: Figure Technologies reported revenue growing over 100% year-over-year with EBITDA up more than 50%, a 'rule of 150' profile that only a couple of other large public companies in the world currently meet.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano (host)
insights.so_what: A rare growth-plus-profitability screen; if the rule-of-150 cohort is genuinely two or three names globally, Figure deserves scarcity-premium treatment.

insights.claim: Collapsing a 30-to-60-day property closing into a same-day tokenized settlement mechanically raises GDP and corporate earnings by increasing the number of transactions per period, while simultaneously being deflationary because the disintermediated price is lower.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: The tokenization thesis is really a velocity-of-money trade — it produces growth and disinflation at the same time, which is the single most bullish macro combination for equities.
insights.quote: The velocity of money, the velocity of transactions is going to increase significantly.

insights.claim: Visser is constructing an index that combines crypto tokens sorted by future-economy vertical with already-public intersection companies — Figure, Robinhood, PayPal, and Coinbase — as the vehicle for the AI-meets-crypto growth wave.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A concrete public-market expression of the tokenization thesis that does not require buying tokens directly — these four are the named liquid proxies.
insights.quote: this intersection is going to be one of the most explosive growth points we've seen because these companies are going to be disrupting from the middle men that cost you time and money every single day

insights.claim: AI agents cannot transact at speed until wallets, money rails, and regulatory guardrails exist, which puts the full agentic-crypto convergence two to three years out and makes Clarity Act progress the specific gate for hedge fund capital entering the space.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Regulatory clarity is the catalyst to watch for institutional flows; the trade has a two-to-three-year runway rather than being an immediate re-rating.
insights.quote: It might take another 2 years, 3 years. And this is why the regulatory side clarity act has an impact on hedge funds looking at this.

insights.claim: Visser dismisses current Bitcoin price weakness, Clarity Act uncertainty, and Fed hike fears as noise inside an intact secular trend, and predicts everyone will be paying attention to crypto within a year.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A stated buy-the-drawdown posture on crypto with a roughly twelve-month horizon for renewed attention and flows.
insights.quote: Mark my words, you will all be paying attention to crypto a year from now.

insights.claim: Figure's rise to third-largest HELOC originator in the country came from Plaid bank-account connections and conventional automation rather than from blockchain — it could approve a HELOC in five minutes and fund in about five days.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano (host)
insights.so_what: The moat is user experience and data plumbing, not the chain — meaning the same disruption is replicable by any operator willing to rebuild the workflow, and blockchain-purity is not the right screen.

insights.claim: Figure's founder Mike Cagney bootstrapped demand for a decentralized DTCC-style settlement layer by originating loans himself and selling them onward, solving the cold-start problem when no counterparty believed the technology had value.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano (host)
insights.so_what: A reusable pattern for evaluating infrastructure startups: the ones that vertically integrate to seed their own marketplace escape the chicken-and-egg trap that kills most protocol plays.

insights.claim: Robinhood now runs seven or eight separate lines of business each generating at least $100 million of revenue, showing that fintech disruptors are compounding through business-line proliferation rather than single-product scale.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano (host)
insights.so_what: Valuing Robinhood as a brokerage understates it; the correct comp set is a multi-product financial platform with optionality in each vertical.

themes.theme: Incumbent Bureaucracy as a Relative Short

insights.claim: JP Morgan is a relative short against Figure and other token-native firms — not because its business is bad, but because its accumulated legacy employees and acquisition-built bureaucracy mean it can only grow at human speed.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A pairs-trade formulation: long token-native financial disruptors against the money-center banks, on organizational metabolic rate rather than credit or rate cycles.
insights.quote: It's not that their business isn't good. It's that they can only grow at human speed.

insights.claim: Google qualifies as a bureaucracy despite growing revenue over 30%, evidenced by Jeff Dean's departure and reports that Demis Hassabis was going to leave — a warning that revenue growth no longer proves organizational health.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Senior AI-talent attrition is a forward indicator to monitor on megacap tech that current financials will not reveal for several quarters.
insights.quote: Because Google is a bureaucracy. Think about that, guys. A company that is growing their revenues at 30 plus percent is a bureaucracy.

insights.claim: Salesforce illustrates how hard the conversion is even for a software company — it is an AI company selling agentic products and still struggling to make the transition.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Being nominally in the AI business is not protection; check whether an incumbent's own operations run at AI speed before crediting it with AI exposure.

insights.claim: Ford is the archetype of the trapped incumbent — an old company loaded with debt and pensions that cannot grow revenue, versus Micron whose earnings compound far faster.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Legacy liabilities (debt, pensions) are the mechanical constraint on incumbent reinvention — screen for them when sizing the AI-disruption short book.

insights.claim: Visser frames the S&P 500 itself as the index of middlemen, with companies like Figure existing specifically to disrupt them, so AI-native firms will eventually disrupt the public companies rather than the reverse.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Passive S&P exposure is increasingly a short on disintermediation — the case for active tilt toward the disruptors rather than index beta.
insights.quote: The companies like Figure are not middle men. They are actually trying to disrupt that business

insights.claim: Visser positions his portfolio in the receivers of AI infrastructure spending rather than the applications, because their earnings are currently growing far faster than the incumbents being disrupted.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Explicit sequencing: own the picks-and-shovels now, rotate to the AI-native disruptors later as the tokenized rails mature.
insights.quote: That's why the portfolio that I put together is the receivers of the infrastructure right now, and their earnings are growing far faster.

themes.theme: LLM Labs, ARR Math and Terminal Value

insights.claim: The greatest risk to Anthropic's valuation is not failing to reach a trillion in ARR but landing at only $200 billion next year, because a discernible slowdown in the growth rate collapses terminal value and compresses the multiple sharply.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: For pre-IPO AI labs the relevant risk metric is second derivative of revenue, not absolute scale — a lab that merely doubles gets repriced downward.
insights.quote: the biggest risk to Anthropic is not whether their ARR gets to a trillion dollars next year. It's probably more if they're only at 200 billion next year. Their valuation's going to come down sharply

insights.claim: ARR is itself a human-time construct that becomes misleading for AI labs — annualizing a final month of roughly $10 billion into a $120 billion headline hides whether monthly growth is actually decelerating.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Demand monthly sequential revenue from AI labs before underwriting an IPO; the annualized headline is engineered to obscure the deceleration.
insights.quote: The reason I emphasize the ARR, you know what that is? That's human time.

insights.claim: Anthropic's revenue is dominated by large Fortune 500 corporates trying to replace employees with LLMs, while AI-native businesses do not consume frontier models the same way — a customer-base concentration in exactly the cohort Visser expects to be disrupted.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Frontier-lab revenue quality is tied to incumbent enterprise budgets; if the incumbents lose share to AI-natives, the labs' customer base erodes with them.
insights.quote: Anthropic's revenues are being dominated by the big companies, the big Fortune 500 companies, the middle men trying to figure a way to replace their employees with the LLMs.

insights.claim: Ordinary businesses only need roughly 150-IQ capability to replace human labor and are better served by open-source models fine-tuned on their own data, while 2,000-IQ frontier models are only necessary for governments, science, and genuinely complex systems.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Bifurcates the AI market: commodity inference for enterprise workflows versus a narrow high-value frontier segment — a bearish read on frontier-lab TAM assumptions.
insights.quote: for running a business where you're just trying to have revenues that are higher than expense, you probably don't need to have 2,000 IQs

insights.claim: Palantir is growing revenue at 149% off a base still under roughly a billion dollars, which Visser uses as the benchmark for what 'growing close to the pace of AI' looks like when assessing whether a name deserves terminal value.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Sets an explicit growth hurdle: anything not compounding near AI-native rates faces multiple compression regardless of absolute quality.

insights.claim: Four or five investors have told Pompliano they are deliberately sitting in cash waiting to deploy into large language model labs when they go public, rather than stay invested and incur taxes on a forced sale.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano (host)
insights.so_what: A pool of pre-committed sidelined capital implies aggressive first-day pricing on any frontier-lab listing and a possible bid vacuum in whatever they would otherwise have owned.

insights.claim: Anthropic is rumored to be tightening its belt ahead of a possible public listing within months while OpenAI has seen a wave of executive departures, with speculation that OpenAI is forcing some of the personnel changes.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano (host)
insights.so_what: Cost discipline plus exec churn is the standard pre-IPO tell; positions expression the AI-lab listing window as near-term rather than years away.

insights.claim: Pompliano treats his wife's adoption of an AI household-manager agent — after months of using AI only as a Google replacement — as the non-technical indicator that AI has hit true product-market fit, arguing that once the technology reaches mothers it is irreversible.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano (host)
insights.so_what: Consumer agent adoption in non-technical households is the demand leg that underwrites another two to three years of the AI capex and equity trade.
insights.quote: when you get to the moms, it's over. Like the technology's not going away. It has finally reached the like product market fit

insights.claim: Public sentiment is shifting from 'data centers are bad, AI takes jobs' toward recognizing everyday benefits, with Facebook and Anthropic softening their messaging toward 'team human' — which Pompliano reads as a major tailwind for AI equities because resistance at every step disappears.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano (host)
insights.so_what: Reduced political and social friction lowers the regulatory discount currently embedded in AI infrastructure names.

insights.claim: Visser argues the productive use of AI is conversational and iterative — repeatedly asking 'but why' — rather than search-style answer retrieval, and that treating model output as truth rather than opinion is the core user error.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Explains why measured enterprise AI ROI lags capability — the adoption bottleneck is usage pattern, which favors products that structure dialogue over those that return answers.
insights.quote: When you use Google, you're getting you're searching for answers, and then you get that answer and you think that's the answer.

insights.claim: Visser describes a 'mosaic thinking' framework in which every decision carries multiple trade-offs rather than a single outcome, and says many of the charts in his research are now produced by AI doing the work for him.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Sell-side and independent research production costs are already collapsing via AI — a margin and competitive-entry story for the research industry itself.

themes.theme: Politics, Immigration and Data Centers as Noise

insights.claim: Visser argues the market is driven by earnings and AI rather than political, religious, or war debates, and that anyone allocating either bullishly or bearishly because of immigration enforcement is wrong.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: An explicit instruction to strip political overlays out of the allocation process and keep the signal set to earnings growth and AI adoption.
insights.quote: The market is moving on earnings. The market is moving on what's happening with AI, and political issues, religious debates, war debates.

insights.claim: University of Michigan consumer confidence sitting at all-time lows is an artifact of partisan composition — Republicans currently score far higher than Democrats and the readings would simply flip under a Democratic president — making the series useless for investing.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Discard UMich sentiment as a recession input; record-low confidence coexisting with record-high equities is a measurement problem, not a divergence to trade.

insights.claim: US immigration authorities removed more than 350,000 individuals so far in fiscal year 2026 with roughly 65,000 still in detention and 60% of those holding criminal records, tracking toward over 400,000 by the September 30 fiscal year end at an average near 1,400 arrests per day in June.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano (host)
insights.so_what: Against a 330 million population these are small absolute numbers, arguing the deportation-as-macro-shock thesis is overstated at the national level even if locally visible.

insights.claim: Visser declines to call deportations inflationary or deflationary because the effect is washed out by simultaneous forces — AI acceleration and digital employees entering the workforce — and because published statistics on both sides are produced with agendas.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Labor-supply shock models are unusable when digital labor supply is expanding at the same time; do not build an inflation view on immigration data.

insights.claim: Visser identifies the political backlash against AI — citing Bernie Sanders's statement targeting Anthropic and OpenAI and efforts to stop data centers — as the actual force disrupting the stock market, while noting the physical build-out is still proceeding.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Political risk to AI, not fundamentals, is the identified source of multiple compression — watch legislative escalation as the real de-rating catalyst.
insights.quote: I deal with the facts of are the data centers still being plugged in? Yes.

insights.claim: Texas's collaborative slowdown on data centers drew agreement from physical builders like Caruso and Hut 8, a markedly different posture from software AI companies' abrasiveness toward government and from New York's blanket ban.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano (host)
insights.so_what: Jurisdiction and posture are becoming differentiators for data center developers — builders that cooperate with regulators face lower siting risk than software firms fighting them.

insights.claim: Visser frames opposition friction as productive creative destruction — every objection forces a better solution, and with AI generating ideas faster the cycle of complaint and workaround accelerates rather than resolves.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Regulatory pushback should be modeled as a routing constraint on capex (underground, offshore, space) rather than as a cap on total AI infrastructure spend.
insights.quote: That is what creative destruction is is you actually need the friction, the not agreeing to come up with a better idea
